title: Grid Challenge
directAnswer: Sort the characters of each row independently in ascending order, then check that every COLUMN is non-decreasing top to bottom. If all columns pass, print 'YES'; otherwise 'NO'. The greedy claim — sorting each row is the best possible arrangement — is provably safe: if any per-row reordering makes the columns sorted, sorting each row ascending does too. O(n · m log m) from sorting the rows.

You may NOT reorder rows or columns as units — only the characters inside each row.
Sorting each row ascending is the unique best try: if any arrangement sorts the columns, the all-rows-ascending one does too.
Compare characters directly (lexicographic / ASCII). All-lowercase input means a plain char comparison works.

You suspect 'sort each part, then verify the global condition' collapses the search

remember.takeaway: When each row can be permuted independently and you need columns to be sorted, the greedy normal form is 'sort every row ascending'. The exchange argument proves it dominates every other per-row arrangement — a clean example of reducing a search over permutations to a single canonical choice.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise sorting each row independently is not just a heuristic but provably optimal for making the columns sortable, and whether you implement the column check correctly.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting the whole grid or sorting columns, or only checking adjacent characters within rows instead of verifying the columns after sorting.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Prove the greedy is safe: if some per-row reordering makes all columns non-decreasing, then replacing each row with its ascending sort preserves that, so the ascending-sort arrangement is a valid witness whenever one exists.

problemStatement:
Given a square grid of lowercase letters represented as `n` strings each of length `n` (more generally `n` rows of length `m`), determine whether the grid can be arranged so that **both** of the following hold:

1. Each **row** is sorted in non-decreasing (ascending) order, and
2. Each **column** is sorted in non-decreasing (top-to-bottom) order.

You may rearrange the characters **within each row** in any order, but you may not move characters between rows. Return `"YES"` if such an arrangement exists, otherwise `"NO"`.
constraints: Each row has the same length m (1 ≤ m ≤ 100)
All characters are lowercase English letters 'a'–'z'
understanding: Since we may freely permute the letters inside any row, the only way to satisfy 'rows sorted ascending' is to actually sort each row. The real question is whether, once every row is sorted ascending, the columns happen to be non-decreasing as well. If yes, the grid is feasible.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I rearrange characters across different rows?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Reordering is allowed only within a row. Characters stay in their original row.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do rows have to be sorted, or just the columns?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both. But because we control the row order completely, satisfying 'rows ascending' is free — sort them. The columns are what may or may not work out.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the grid always square?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The classic version is n × n, but the algorithm works for any n × m: sort each length-m row, then check the columns.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are characters case-sensitive or include non-letters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: All lowercase English letters, so a direct character (ASCII) comparison is enough.

examples.explanation: Sort each row → ["abcde", "fghij", "klmno", "pqrst", "uvwxy"]. Every column reads top-to-bottom as a,f,k,p,u … all non-decreasing.
Rows already ascending. Columns: (a,a,e), (b,d,f), (c,e,g) — each non-decreasing → YES.
Sort each row → ["xyz", "uvw"]. Column 0 is (x,u): u < x, so it decreases → NO.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Every Per-Row Permutation
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it to expose the search space, then collapse it with the 'sort each row' lemma.
hints: Each row can be permuted in m! ways. A full arrangement is one permutation per row — how many combinations is that across n rows?
Enumerate every combination of per-row permutations, then check whether all columns are non-decreasing. Return YES if any combination works.
This is astronomically large — (m!)ⁿ. It's only useful to argue that we don't need it: a single canonical permutation (sort ascending) suffices.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are m! permutations per row and n rows, so (m!)ⁿ combinations; verifying each scans the n×m grid. The exponential tower makes it infeasible past trivial sizes.
approaches.explanation:
Brute force takes the problem at face value: 'rearrange characters within each row' means each row has `m!` possible orderings, and an arrangement of the whole grid picks one ordering per row. We'd enumerate all `(m!)ⁿ` combinations and, for each, test whether every column is non-decreasing top to bottom.

**Why this is the literal reading.** The problem grants a freedom (permute within rows) and asks a yes/no question (can the columns be made sorted). The exhaustive way to answer is to try every legal arrangement and check the property.

**Why it's impossible at scale.** With `m = 100` the per-row count `100!` is already larger than the number of atoms in the universe, and we raise that to the `n`-th power. No machine enumerates this.

**The lemma that rescues us.** Claim: *if any combination of per-row permutations makes all columns non-decreasing, then sorting every row ascending also makes all columns non-decreasing.* Intuitively, sorting a row ascending only ever moves smaller characters left and larger ones right; doing this to every row preserves the existence of a valid column ordering. So we never need to search — one canonical arrangement (all rows ascending) is a valid witness whenever any witness exists. That turns `(m!)ⁿ` into a single sort per row.
approaches.insight: The brute force's only value is revealing that the feasibility property is closed under sorting each row. Once you believe that lemma, the entire permutation search collapses to a single canonical arrangement.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort Each Row Ascending, Then Check Columns (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'sort every row, then a single pass verifies the columns'.
hints: Rows can be freely permuted, so satisfying 'rows ascending' costs nothing — just sort them. What's left to verify?
After sorting each row ascending, the only thing that can still fail is a column decreasing somewhere. Check each column top to bottom.
If every adjacent pair grid[i][j] >= grid[i-1][j] holds for all columns, return YES; the first violation returns NO.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting n rows of length m is O(n · m log m) and dominates; the column scan is O(n · m). We store the mutable sorted rows → O(n · m) space.
approaches.explanation:
Two phases. **Phase 1: sort each row ascending.** Since the problem lets us reorder characters within a row, and 'rows must be ascending' is one of the requirements, sorting each row is both *required* and *free*. **Phase 2: verify columns.** Walk every column top to bottom; if any `grid[i][j] < grid[i-1][j]`, the column decreases and the grid is infeasible — return `"NO"`. If all columns survive, return `"YES"`.

**Why sorting each row is safe — the exchange argument.** Suppose some arrangement `A` (one permutation per row) makes all columns non-decreasing. Take any single row of `A` that isn't already ascending; it has two adjacent positions `j` and `j+1` with `A[i][j] > A[i][j+1]`. Swap them. After the swap the row is 'more sorted', and crucially the columns are still valid: at column `j` the value only got smaller (helps the `≤` from above and still dominates below because the value that moved in came from a position that was already column-valid), and symmetrically at `j+1`. Repeating adjacent swaps (a bubble sort) turns every row ascending while preserving column validity at each step. Therefore, if *any* valid arrangement exists, the all-rows-ascending arrangement is valid too. So we lose nothing by committing to ascending rows — the greedy choice can never rule out a feasible grid.

**Why we still must check columns.** Sorting rows fixes the row requirement but says nothing about columns. `["zyx", "wvu"]` sorts to `["xyz", "uvw"]`, yet column 0 reads `x` then `u` — a decrease. The column scan is the actual feasibility decision; the sort just puts us in the only arrangement worth testing.

**Why top-to-bottom adjacent comparison suffices.** Non-decreasing down a column is a transitive chain: if every consecutive pair satisfies `≥`, the whole column is sorted. We never need to compare non-adjacent rows.
approaches.insight: The freedom 'permute within rows' has a unique canonical resolution: sort ascending. Recognising that a search over arrangements has one dominating representative — and proving it with a swap argument — is the reusable skill. After that, the problem is a trivial monotonicity scan.

pitfalls: Sorting the entire flattened grid instead of each row separately.
Checking only rows after sorting and forgetting the column scan.
Comparing non-adjacent rows — adjacent comparisons already cover the whole column by transitivity.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to verify the columns after sorting the rows.
Sorting the whole grid or attempting to sort columns directly.
Assuming rows can exchange characters with other rows.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the column verification
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Sorting rows satisfies only the row requirement. Without the column scan, a grid like ["zyx","wvu"] would be wrongly accepted.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
rows = [sorted(row) for row in grid]
return "YES"

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting the grid as one flat list
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Characters may only move within their own row. Flattening and sorting the whole grid moves characters across rows, which is illegal.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing within a row instead of down a column
commonMistakesDetailed.why: After sorting, rows are trivially non-decreasing. The real condition couples rows together, so you must compare grid[i][j] against grid[i-1][j] down each column.

patternNote: Greedy normalisation under per-row freedom: when each row can be permuted independently and you must satisfy a cross-row monotonic property, sorting every row ascending is the dominating canonical arrangement. Prove it with a bubble-swap exchange argument, then the problem reduces to a single column-monotonicity scan.
